passages.t: A second sign child, and the river of Assyria
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Isaiah to take a large scroll and write on it, ‘Maher-shalal-hash-baz’ (verse 1), with two trustworthy witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah (verse 2). Isaiah's wife, the prophetess, gives birth to a son, and the LORD tells him to give the boy that name (verse 3). Before the child can say Father or Mother, ‘the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria’ (verse 4).

Because this people ‘has rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah’ (verse 6), the Lord will bring against them ‘the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates’ (verse 7), the king of Assyria in all his pomp. It will pour into Judah and sweep over it, ‘reaching up to the neck; its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel’ (verse 8).

Then a defiant poem to the nations: band together and be shattered, plan and be thwarted, ‘For God is with us’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The events still belong to the crisis of about 734 to 732 BC. The long name Maher-shalal-hash-baz means roughly swift to the spoil, quick to the plunder. Writing it on a scroll before witnesses was like registering a public document: when the events came, the witnesses could confirm that Isaiah had said it in advance. Before the boy could talk, Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC and stripped Israel of much of its land. Uriah the priest is probably the priest who later built a copy of the altar Ahaz had seen in Damascus.

The gently flowing waters of Shiloah were probably a channel carrying water from the Gihon spring along the Kidron Valley to the south of the city. They stand for God's quiet, unimpressive care in Jerusalem, set against the mighty Euphrates, the river of Assyria. The New Testament's Siloam takes its name from Shiloah.

The name Immanuel appears twice. At the end of verse 8 it is a cry, as the flood reaches the neck of the land. At the end of verse 10 the Hebrew for ‘God is with us’ (verse 10) spells the same name, as a confession. The flood is real, and so is the God who is with his people.
passages.later: Jesus sent a blind man to ‘wash in the Pool of Siloam’ (John 9:7), the pool whose water came from these same springs. And a generation after Isaiah, Hezekiah cut ‘the tunnel to bring water into the city’ (2 Kings 20:20), which brought the Gihon's water inside the walls.
passages.asks: Judah rejected the gently flowing waters for the mighty river. Ask where you have preferred impressive help to God's quiet provision. And ask whether you can confess that God is with his people in the middle of a flood, as Isaiah did.

passages.t: Fear the LORD, the sanctuary and the stone
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Isaiah ‘with a strong hand’ (verse 11), warning him not to walk in the way of this people. ‘Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy. Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread’ (verse 12).

‘The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded’ (verse 13). He will be a sanctuary, but to both houses of Israel ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense’ (verse 14), and a trap and snare to Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall and be broken (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is a private word to Isaiah. Jerusalem was full of fear and rumor in the war years, and everyone was talking about plots. Isaiah is told not to share the panic. The only one worth fearing is the LORD.

The same God is two things at once. To those who trust him, he is a sanctuary, a place of refuge. To those who refuse him, he is a stone that trips them. The first hearers were being told that God would not be neutral. They would find in him either shelter or stumbling.

The chapter is turning from the public stage to the prophet's small circle. The king has refused to listen. Isaiah will now gather those who will.
passages.later: Peter quotes these words to Christians under pressure: ‘Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken’ (1 Peter 3:14), and goes on, ‘in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord’ (1 Peter 3:15). Paul and Peter both join verse 14 to Isaiah 28:16 to speak of Christ: ‘See, I lay in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense’ (Romans 9:33).
passages.asks: Isaiah was told not to fear what everyone around him feared. Ask what fear your own community is passing around that you have caught. And ask whether God is a sanctuary to you or a stone you keep tripping over.

passages.t: The testimony sealed, and the dead not consulted
passages.happening:
‘Bind up the testimony and seal the law among my disciples’ (verse 16). Isaiah will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and put his trust in him (verse 17). ‘Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel’ (verse 18).

When people tell them to consult the spirits of the dead and the spiritists who whisper and mutter, should not a people consult their God instead? ‘Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?’ (verse 19). “To the law and to the testimony!” (verse 20). If they do not speak by this word, they have no dawn.

They will roam the land hungry and angry, cursing their king and their God (verse 21). They will look to the earth and see only distress and darkness, and be driven into utter darkness (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Rejected by the king, Isaiah turns to a small band of disciples who will keep his teaching until God acts. Binding and sealing was what one did with a legal document, to keep it safe and unaltered. Isaiah's words are preserved for the day they are proved true. Isaiah's children, with their message names, are signs too.

Consulting the dead was widespread in the ancient world and strictly forbidden in Israel's law. Mediums claimed to call up spirits, thought to speak in faint whispering or muttering voices; the Hebrew words describe that sound. King Saul's visit to the medium at Endor is the Bible's best-known example. Isaiah's point is simple: why go to the dead for guidance about the living, when the living God has spoken?

The chapter ends in darkness, which makes the light at the start of chapter 9 all the more striking.
passages.later: The letter to the Hebrews puts verses 17 and 18 on the lips of Christ: ‘I will put My trust in Him’ and ‘Here am I, and the children God has given Me’ (Hebrews 2:13). The law had forbidden anyone who ‘consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead’ (Deuteronomy 18:11).
passages.hard:
Why does the chapter forbid consulting the dead, and what happens when people try?

In the ancient world, seeking knowledge from the dead was a regular part of religious life, and ancient texts describe rituals for contacting spirits. Israel's law banned it, along with divination and sorcery, because it sought guidance and power apart from God and treated the dead as sources of revelation. Isaiah's argument is about God, not technique: his people should consult their God, whose word is found in his law and testimony.

The Bible does not give a full account of what happens in such practices. The story of Saul and the medium of Endor is read by some as a real appearance of Samuel permitted by God and by others as a deception, and the text leaves its details unexplained. What the Bible says consistently is that such practices are forbidden and spiritually dangerous, and that the living God has spoken clearly enough for his people to walk in the light.

Grief can make people long to hear a voice they have lost. That longing is human, and God does not despise it.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Isaiah chose to wait for a God who was hiding his face, and to trust him. Ask whether you can wait like that when God seems silent. And ask where you go for guidance when God's word feels too slow.
